x: Citizenship is in Part II, Articles 5–11, which identifies citizens at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950). Part III (12–35) is Fundamental Rights and Part I (1–4) the Union and its territory.
t: Link citizenship to Part II.

x: Article 5 – citizenship at commencement; Article 6 – migrants from Pakistan to India; Article 7 – migrants to Pakistan; Article 8 – persons of Indian origin abroad.
t: Follow the order: commencement, from Pakistan, to Pakistan, abroad.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Parliament's exclusive power over citizenship comes from Article 11, which lets it legislate on acquisition, termination and all related matters.
t: Check whether R is the source of the power in A.

x: B is incorrect: the Election Commission has no power over citizenship; Parliament alone regulates it under Article 11 (Citizenship Act, 1955, with Rules under Section 18).
t: Spot the body wrongly given legislative power.

x: Both are true: India has single citizenship and a single domicile for the whole country — unitary features of its federal structure (unlike the US dual citizenship).
t: Recall single citizenship as a unitary feature.

x: Article 5 conferred citizenship on persons domiciled in India who were born in India, had a parent born in India, or had lived in India for at least five years before 1950. Two years and property ownership are distractors.
t: Recall the five-year residence condition of Article 5.

x: Birth – place of birth (jus soli); Descent – born abroad to Indian parents; Registration – includes a PIO ordinarily resident for seven years; Naturalisation – foreigners meeting residence and character criteria.
t: Match each mode to its basis.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Section 10 lets the Central Government compulsorily deprive a naturalised or registered citizen of citizenship on grounds such as fraud or disloyalty.
t: Check whether R is the provision behind A.

x: I, II and III are correct: birth, descent and incorporation of territory are modes of acquiring citizenship (with registration and naturalisation). Criticising the government is no mode at all.
t: Recall the five modes B-D-R-N-I.

x: Renunciation – voluntary surrender; Termination – automatic loss on voluntarily taking foreign citizenship; Deprivation – compulsory termination by the Central Government; Article 9 – constitutional basis for loss on acquiring foreign citizenship.
t: Separate voluntary, automatic and compulsory loss.

x: C is incorrect: voluntary surrender is renunciation; deprivation is compulsory termination by the Central Government. The other descriptions are right.
t: Match each mode of loss to who acts.

x: Unlawful trading with an enemy during war is a ground for deprivation under Section 10. Marrying a foreigner, criticising the government or buying property abroad do not cost citizenship.
t: Pick the ground that shows disloyalty.

x: Both are true: in India both citizens by birth and naturalised citizens can become President, whereas in the USA only a natural-born citizen can.
t: Compare the two countries' eligibility rules.

x: All four: bank deposits or property in India do not give citizenship, and marrying a foreigner or criticising the government does not by itself take it away.
t: Recognise acts that neither give nor remove citizenship.
s:
How many of the following, by themselves, neither confer Indian citizenship nor cause its loss?

I. Depositing money in Indian banks
II. Purchasing property in India
III. Marrying a foreign citizen
IV. Criticizing the government or its policies

x: Registration is Section 5 of the Citizenship Act, 1955. Section 6 is naturalisation, 7A the OCI scheme and 10 deprivation.
t: Link Section 5 to registration.

x: Article 9 – loss on voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship; Article 10 – continuance of citizenship; Article 11 – Parliament to regulate citizenship; Article 8 – persons of Indian origin abroad.
t: Recall Articles 8 to 11 in order.

x: I, II and III are correct (Article 6's cut-off of 19 July 1948; Article 7's returnees on resettlement permits; Article 8's registration by Indian diplomats abroad). IV is wrong: the legislative power is Article 11; Article 10 only continues citizenship subject to Parliament's laws.
t: Separate continuance (Article 10) from legislative power (Article 11).
s:
Consider the following statements regarding citizenship provisions:
I. Article 6 deals with migration before or after the permit cut-off date of 19 July 1948.
II. Article 7 concerns persons who migrated after 1 March 1947 but later returned under a resettlement permit.
III. Article 8 provides for registration as a citizen by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
IV. Article 10 gives Parliament comprehensive power to enact citizenship legislation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: Entry cut-off 31 December 2014; Lok Sabha passed the CAA on 9 December 2019, Rajya Sabha on 11 December and the President assented on 12 December: D, B, C, A.
t: Place the cut-off date first, then the Act's passage.

x: C is incorrect: persons who were citizens of Pakistan or Bangladesh, or whose parents or grandparents were, are ineligible for OCI registration (Section 7A).
t: Watch for 'without restriction'.

x: All four are correct: the CAA passed the Lok Sabha on 9 December 2019, the Rajya Sabha on 11 December, got assent on 12 December, and covers six non-Muslim minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered by 31 December 2014.
t: Check each date and condition of the CAA.
s:
Consider the following statements about the Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019:
I. The Lok Sabha passed it on 9 December 2019.
II. The Rajya Sabha passed it on 11 December 2019.
III. Presidential Assent was given on 12 December 2019.
IV. It applies to six non-Muslim persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: The Citizenship Rules are made under Section 18 of the Citizenship Act, 1955. Sections 5, 6 and 10 deal with registration, naturalisation and deprivation.
t: Link rule-making to Section 18.

x: Goa's acquisition is an example of citizenship by incorporation of territory (as are Pondicherry and Sikkim). Birth, registration and naturalisation are other modes.
t: Incorporation means India acquiring a new territory.

x: Birth – jus soli; Descent – jus sanguinis; Naturalisation – residence and character criteria; Incorporation – acquisition of a new territory.
t: Soli = soil (birth), sanguinis = blood (descent).

x: Naturalisation is Section 6 of the Citizenship Act, 1955. Section 5 is registration, 7A OCI and 10 deprivation.
t: Link Section 6 to naturalisation.

x: I and III are correct: persons married to Indian citizens may register as citizens, under Section 5. II is wrong: registration is a mode of acquiring citizenship, not losing it.
t: Separate modes of acquisition from modes of loss.
s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Persons married to Indian citizens are included among the categories for registration.
II. Registration is a mode of loss of citizenship.
III. Registration is governed by Section 5 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

x: D is incorrect: marrying a foreign citizen does not by itself cause loss of citizenship. Deprivation is a compulsory termination by the Central Government, on grounds such as fraud.
t: Watch for 'automatically'.

x: All four are grounds for deprivation under Section 10: fraud, disloyalty to the Constitution, unlawful trade with an enemy in war, and two years' imprisonment within five years of naturalisation or registration.
t: Recall the grounds of compulsory deprivation.

x: The OCI Cardholder scheme is in Section 7A of the Citizenship Act. Sections 5, 6 and 18 cover registration, naturalisation and rules.
t: Link OCI to Section 7A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the countries and the cut-off date are eligibility conditions; they do not explain why the Act covers six non-Muslim minorities.
t: Eligibility conditions do not explain the choice of groups.

x: C is incorrect: the CAA covers those who entered India on or before 31 December 2014, not after. The other statements are right.
t: Check 'on or before' against 'after'.

x: Part II identified citizens as on the commencement of the Constitution, 26 January 1950. 19 July 1948 is Article 6's permit cut-off and 1 March 1947 Article 7's migration date.
t: Separate the commencement date from Partition cut-off dates.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 10 continues every person's citizenship, subject to any law Parliament makes.
t: Check whether R restates the content of Article 10.

x: Both are true: only Parliament can make citizenship laws (Article 11); neither State Legislatures nor the President have that power.
t: Remember Parliament's exclusive power.

x: Both are true: the USA has dual (federal and state) citizenship, while India's automatic loss of citizenship on taking a foreign one reflects its single-citizenship rule.
t: Contrast dual and single citizenship.

x: All four are correct: B-D-R-N-I stands for Birth, Descent, Registration, Naturalisation and Incorporation of territory; Pondicherry, Sikkim and Goa are examples of incorporation.
t: Recall the mnemonic and the three incorporated territories.

x: Both are true: R-T-D stands for Renunciation, Termination and Deprivation, the modes of loss; Article 58 lays down qualifications for election as President.
t: Recall the loss mnemonic.
